> 须菩提白佛言：「世尊！颇有众生，得闻如是言说章句，生实信不？」佛告须菩提：「莫作是说。如来灭后，后五百岁，有持戒修福者，于此章句能生信心。」

The sixth section begins with doubt, and the doubt is ours.

须菩提 asks whether anyone, hearing sentences like these, will actually believe them. It is not a rhetorical courtesy. It is the question every reader has already had: this teaching is too strange, too demanding, and the people who will hear it are not the people who heard the Buddha.

The answer is the most encouraging sentence in the sutra, and it is aimed precisely at that worry.

## 后五百岁 is an argument against nostalgia

The tradition divides the age after the Buddha's death into periods: a thousand years of true dharma, a thousand of semblance, then a long decline. 后五百岁 — the fifth five-hundred-year span — is placed in the period of contention and thickening affliction, the worst of the timetable.

The Buddha names that period and says: there will be people then who believe this.

Which dismantles a reflex that is still with us: *people nowadays are not capable; the old practitioners were; this is a degraded age.* The sutra's answer is that difficulty is not disqualification. If anything, the section treats the hard age as the test case.

## 持戒修福 comes before 能生信心

Note the order. First keeping precepts, then cultivating merit, *then* the capacity for faith.

Faith here is not a mood and not a gift. It has a floor under it: conduct and generosity. A person whose life is unmanaged, who takes what is not given and says what is not true, does not have the stillness in which a sentence like *do not abide anywhere* can land. The ground is prepared by behaviour.

This is worth saying plainly because "faith" in modern usage is almost weightless — an opinion you hold. In this text it is a capacity that gets built.

## 一念净信 is rare because it must hold two things at once

净信 — pure faith — is defined by what it is free of: the four signs, the mark of dharma, and the mark of non-dharma.

That third clause is the difficult one. Not holding "things exist" is one skill. Not holding "nothing exists" is another. Holding neither, in the same instant, is why 一念 — a single moment — is the unit of measure here, and why the section calls such a person rare.

The book is blunt: this has nothing to do with being moved. A person can weep at a dharma talk and still be holding both ends. A single instant in which neither end is held is worth more than the tears.

## 法尚应舍, and the raft

The section's closing image is the raft: the teaching is a boat for crossing, and once across, it is left on the bank.

Everyone quotes this to justify discarding something — texts, rituals, teachers, lineage. The book's correction is exact: what is left behind is the *grip*, not the *teaching*. Abandoning the raft mid-river is not detachment, it is drowning with a good theory.

## 善根 is cultivation, not fate

The passage says such people have planted roots with countless buddhas. It is easy to hear this as predestination: some are born able to believe, others are not.

But 善根 is cultivated — the three healthy roots of non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, watered over time. This morning's sentence heard, this afternoon's small act of restraint: that is planting. The sentence is not a report on your fixed nature. It is a description of what accumulates when someone keeps at it.

## The test

Ask the question 须菩提 asked, but make it first-person: what would I have to give up in order to actually believe this?

Not to agree with it — belief of the agreeing kind is cheap. To act as if it were true for one day: give without tracking, sit without needing the result.

If the answer is "nothing", you have not understood the sentence yet. If the answer is a specific thing, you have located the 善根 that still needs watering.
